content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Juice, NFS is a 100 % natural fruit juice specially formulated for children from 1 year old. It is made from selected apples, pears and carrots, without added sugar, preservatives or artificial flavors. The product undergoes strict quality control and meets infant nutrition standards.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The juice is produced from fruits grown without pesticides.
Each bottle contains exactly 150 ml, an optimal portion for toddler feeding.
It provides vitamin C, which supports the child’s immune system.
No added sugar – sweetness comes from the natural sugars of the fruits.
The packaging is made from recyclable PET, reducing environmental impact.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C helps strengthen the immune system and improves iron absorption.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Pectin from apples and pears aids regular bowel movements.

items.title: Source of beta‑carotene
items.content: Carrots provide provitamin A, essential for vision and growth.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: The juice is suitable for children who need to limit salt intake.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Helps maintain fluid balance, especially in warm weather.

items.title: Fruit allergy
items.content: Children with known allergies to apples, pears or carrots should avoid this product.

items.title: Not for infants under 1 year
items.content: The juice may be too heavy for the digestive system of babies younger than one year.

items.title: Natural sugar content
items.content: Although no sugar is added, the product still contains fructose; moderate consumption is advised.

items.title: Post‑opening storage
items.content: After opening, the juice should be consumed within 24 hours to prevent fermentation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the juice chilled or at room temperature. Offer small portions (30–50 ml) several times a day, combined with other toddler foods.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within one day.

content.title: About
content.content: Whole‑grain bread is a baked product made from whole‑grain wheat flour, which retains the bran and germ portions of the kernel. This gives the loaf a richer flavor, denser texture, and higher levels of dietary fiber, vitamins, and minerals compared with white bread.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain bread is often labeled “healthy” because of its high fiber content.
It is frequently enriched with seeds such as sunflower, flax, or pumpkin for extra nutrition.
Traditional Russian whole‑grain loaves are baked in deeper pans, resulting in a thick crust that locks in moisture.
B‑vitamin levels are higher in whole‑grain bread than in refined white bread.
The denser crumb slows starch crystallization, helping the bread stay fresh longer.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, and folate aid energy metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Magnesium, iron, and zinc from whole‑grain flour are essential for muscle function and immunity.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Whole‑grain bread raises blood glucose more slowly, which is beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Heart‑friendly
items.content: Fiber and plant phytochemicals help lower LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: Wheat allergy / gluten intolerance
items.content: Individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity may experience serious reactions to bread.

items.title: High carbohydrate content
items.content: Overconsumption can contribute to weight gain, especially in sedentary individuals.

items.title: Phytic acid presence
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or fermenting the dough lowers its level.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Whole‑grain bread works well for sandwiches, toast, and as a side to soups and salads. It can be toasted, turned into croutons, or used for breadcrumbs. Pair it with lean proteins, vegetables, and healthy fats for a balanced meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the loaf in a paper bag or cloth sack at room temperature to keep the crust crisp. For longer storage (over 3‑4 days), place it in an airtight container in the refrigerator or freeze it; reheat in the oven before serving.

breakfast-bar-date-with-yogurt-coating.title: Breakfast Bar, Date, with Yogurt Coating

content.title: About
content.content: The Breakfast Bar, Date, with Yogurt Coating is an energy snack made from dates, nuts, and whole grains, covered with a smooth yogurt glaze. It combines the natural sweetness of dates, the crunch of nuts, and a light tang of yogurt for a satisfying taste and quick energy boost.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dates are a natural source of simple sugars that are quickly absorbed for instant energy.
The yogurt coating contains probiotics that may support a healthy gut microbiome.
No added sugar is used; sweetness comes entirely from the dates.
The bar includes nuts rich in healthy fats and whole grains that increase fiber content.
Individually wrapped portions make it convenient for on‑the‑go snacking.

items.title: Rapid energy source
items.content: Dates provide glucose and fructose that quickly enter the bloodstream, raising energy levels.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Fiber from dates and whole grains promotes intestinal motility and regular bowel movements.

items.title: Probiotics from yogurt
items.content: The yogurt glaze supplies live cultures that can help maintain a balanced gut flora.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Nuts deliver monounsaturated fats that are beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Dates and nuts provide potassium, magnesium, B‑vitamins, and iron.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: The product contains nuts, which may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Although the sugar is natural, people with diabetes should consider the overall glycemic load.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The bar is relatively calorie‑dense; moderation is important for weight management.

items.title: Probiotic stability
items.content: Yogurt coating may lose live cultures if stored for long periods at high temperatures.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bar as a standalone snack, crumble it into yogurt or oatmeal, or use it as an energy boost before workouts. For a softer glaze, gently warm the bar before eating.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep them in an airtight container or reseal the original packaging tightly. For extended shelf life, refrigeration helps preserve the texture of the yogurt coating.

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen cauliflower cooked with oil is a ready‑to‑eat product made from fresh cauliflower that is blanched, flash‑frozen and then sautéed in vegetable oil. It retains most of its nutrients and has a tender, slightly crisp texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cauliflower belongs to the cruciferous family, along with broccoli, Brussels sprouts and cabbage.
Freezing preserves up to 90 % of vitamin C, which is often lost in fresh produce during storage.
Cooking in oil enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as vitamin K and carotenoids.
Cauliflower can be used as a low‑carb alternative to rice or potatoes in many dishes.
In the United States, frozen vegetables—including cauliflower—are among the top-selling ready‑to‑cook foods.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: One cup provides about 70 kcal, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Compounds such as glucoraphanin help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Oil content
items.content: The product is prepared with vegetable oil, so those monitoring fat intake should consider its caloric contribution.

items.title: Cruciferous allergy
items.content: A small number of people may be allergic to cruciferous vegetables.

items.title: Added salt or preservatives
items.content: Some versions may contain added salt or preservatives; check the label if this is a concern.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to heat: microwave or sauté briefly. Use it in soups, stews, pasta dishes, as a side dish, or as a base for vegetarian patties.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C or lower. After thawing, consume within 2–3 days and do not refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Fat‑free chocolate milk is a beverage made from skimmed cow’s milk (usually less than 0.5 % fat) to which cocoa powder, sugar and flavorings are added. It retains most of the nutrients of regular milk while offering a low‑calorie, smooth chocolate taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Skim milk provides almost the same amount of calcium as whole milk but with roughly half the calories.
The chocolate flavor is achieved by combining cocoa powder with a modest amount of sugar, making it popular among both children and calorie‑conscious adults.
In the United States, fat‑free chocolate milk is often marketed as a post‑workout recovery drink.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Calcium is essential for strong bones and teeth and also supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D enhances calcium absorption and supports the immune system.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein source
items.content: Skim milk provides about 3.4 g of protein per 100 ml, helping maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa powder is high in flavonoids, which may reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience digestive discomfort after consuming dairy products.

items.title: Added sugar content
items.content: Despite being low‑calorie, the drink contains added sugar, which may be a concern for diabetics or those limiting sugar intake.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein or whey protein requires complete avoidance of dairy.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Enjoy chilled as a refreshing drink, blend into smoothies, use in protein shakes, or pour over oatmeal for a chocolate twist.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 1‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days. Avoid freezing, as it can alter the texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Cornbread prepared from mix (2572) is a classic American quick bread made primarily from cornmeal. It has a dense yet crumbly texture, a golden crust, and a subtly sweet, buttery flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cornbread originated in the United States in the 19th century as an easy way to use cornmeal.
Traditionally baked in a rectangular pan, it also appears as muffins or mini loaves.
The mix usually includes leavening agents, salt, sugar, and powdered milk for convenience.
In the Southern states it is commonly served with fried meat, beans, and barbecue sauce.
Cornbread can be sweetened with honey or sugar, or made savory with cheese or herbs.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Cornmeal provides slow‑releasing energy, helping to keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and regular bowel movements.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B3 and folate aid carbohydrate metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Provides magnesium and iron
items.content: These minerals are important for muscle function and blood formation.

items.title: Low in gluten
items.content: For those sensitive to gluten, cornbread can be a more tolerable option, though it is not completely gluten‑free.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Cornbread can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared mixes often contain added salt; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve warm, sliced, as a side to soups, stews, fried meats, or vegetable dishes. Spread with butter, honey, or jam, or use it for sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the baked bread in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate up to a week or freeze wrapped tightly.

content.title: About
content.content: Cucumber and vegetable namasu is a traditional Japanese dish consisting of thinly sliced fresh vegetables (cucumber, carrot, radish, daikon) and seaweed, lightly pickled in a sweet‑sour vinegar dressing with soy sauce, sugar and rice vinegar. The dish is crisp, refreshing and mildly tangy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Namasu is often served as an appetizer (zakuska) in sushi restaurants.
The vegetables are cut into very thin strips to highlight their crunch and allow the dressing to coat each piece evenly.
In Japan the dish is considered festive because its bright colors symbolize joy and prosperity.
Cucumber retains most of its vitamins thanks to the short marinating time.
There are many regional variations that add kelp, ginger or toasted sesame.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Cucumber and carrot provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: With high water content and little fat, namasu fits well into calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrots and other phytochemicals help combat free radicals.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: Cucumber is over 95 % water, helping maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Seaweed allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to seaweed or soy sauce.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The pickling sauce can be salty; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: If non‑organic vegetables are used, residues may be present; thorough washing before marinating is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve namasu chilled as a side dish with sushi, rolls or rice bowls. It can be tossed into salads, used as a roll filling, or simply eaten with a spoon. Before serving, garnish with toasted sesame seeds or finely sliced green onion.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep namasu in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5‑7 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Olives are the fruits of the olive tree (Olea europaea), drupes like cherries or plums. Raw, they are very bitter, so they are soaked, fermented, or cured in brine. Green olives are picked unripe, while black olives are picked ripe or treated in a special way. Olives are eaten as a snack and added to salads, pasta, pizza, sauces, and baked goods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Olives are drupes, yet the olive tree is related to jasmine and lilac.
The bitterness of fresh olives comes from a compound called oleuropein, which is removed during processing.
Green olives are usually picked unripe and black olives fully ripe, but some black olives are produced through special processing.
Olives are stuffed with peppers, cheese, almonds, or anchovies.
Spain is the largest producer of olives.

items.title: Contain monounsaturated fats
items.content: These are heart-friendly fats, the same kind found in olive oil.

items.title: Contain vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E is an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Contain polyphenols
items.content: The polyphenols in olives have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Contain fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and helps you feel full.

items.title: Contain iron and calcium
items.content: In small amounts, olives provide these minerals.

items.title: A lot of salt
items.content: Olives in brine are very salty, so people with high blood pressure should limit portions.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Olives contain a lot of fat, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Pits
items.content: Olives with pits can damage teeth, and they are a choking hazard for small children.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Olive allergy is possible, including in people sensitive to olive tree pollen.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat olives as a snack, or add them to salads, pasta, pizza, stews, and sauces such as tapenade. You can rinse them before eating to wash off some of the salt from the brine. Pitted olives are convenient for cooking, while olives with pits are often tastier.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool place. After opening, keep olives in the refrigerator in a covered container so they stay submerged in brine, and use them within a few weeks. If there is too little brine, top it up with salted water. Discard olives that are moldy or smell off.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork is a protein‑rich meat that provides B‑vitamins and essential minerals. Combined with carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy vegetables (such as spinach or kale), the dish gains extra vitamins A, C, K, as well as fiber, minerals and antioxidants. Prepared without potatoes or soy‑based sauce, it suits those limiting gluten and soy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide.
Broccoli contains sulforaphane, a compound studied for its anti‑cancer properties.
Carrots are high in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Dark‑green leafy greens are rich in chlorophyll and vitamin K.
When paired correctly, protein and vegetables provide a balanced profile of amino acids and micronutrients.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: Pork supplies complete animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: It contains thiamine, riboflavin, niacin and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Broccoli and carrots provide vitamin C, beta‑carotene and sulforaphane, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Fiber and minerals
items.content: Leafy greens and carrots add dietary fiber, potassium, magnesium and iron, beneficial for heart health and digestion.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: The combination of vitamins A, C and zinc from pork and vegetables helps strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Some cuts of pork can be high in saturated fat; choose lean cuts and limit added oil.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Pork should be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C to destroy pathogens.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may experience an allergic reaction to pork.

items.title: Interaction with medication
items.content: High vitamin K levels in leafy greens can affect the efficacy of anticoagulant drugs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté, roast or stew pork with carrots, broccoli and leafy greens. Add a drizzle of olive oil, garlic and your favorite herbs. Serve hot, either with whole‑grain sides or as a standalone plate.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw pork refrigerated at ≤4 °C for 2‑3 days; store cooked dishes in an airtight container for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze the meat in sealed bags and keep vegetables in moisture‑controlled bags.

content.title: About
content.content: Creamed spinach is a ready‑to‑eat product made from fresh spinach blended with a creamy sauce. It has a mild, slightly buttery flavor and a smooth texture, making it a convenient side dish or ingredient.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach is one of the most nutrient‑dense leafy greens.
Creamed spinach is commonly used as a filling for pies, lasagna, and pasta dishes.
The iron content in spinach is higher than most meats, but absorption improves with vitamin C.
Romans traditionally prepared spinach with milk or cream.
Spinach color ranges from bright to dark green depending on variety and growing conditions.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene, which converts to vitamin A, supports vision and immunity.

items.title: Source of iron and magnesium
items.content: Iron transports oxygen in the blood, while magnesium supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from ultraviolet damage.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in spinach promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Spinach contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Leafy‑green allergy
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergic reaction to spinach.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The creamed version often contains added salt; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Creamed spinach can be served as a side, mixed into pasta, risotto, omelets, casseroles, or used as a pie filling. It reheats quickly on the stovetop or in the microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0–4 °C in a sealed container for 3–5 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 2 months. Discard if the product develops an off‑smell or discoloration.
